Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Maharashtra: Ajanta, Ellora and Maratha forts

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Maharashtra has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than almost any Indian state: Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Mumbai's Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles, eleven of the twelve forts of the Maratha Military Landscapes (2025), and part of the Western Ghats. Karla, Bhaja, Kanheri, Daulatabad and Pune add further layers.

We run Mumbai programmes and a multi-day Mumbai tour, and plan Ajanta, Ellora and Maratha fort study tours on request.

Why Maharashtra matters for Indian heritage

The Western Ghats run the length of Maharashtra, and their basalt cliffs were ideal for cutting caves. From about the 2nd century BCE, Buddhist monks and their patrons, many of them traders crossing the passes between the coast and the Deccan plateau, carved monasteries and halls into the rock. Later Hindu and Jain patrons continued the practice, culminating at Ellora. Our guide to Buddhist caves in India explains the forms.

The same hills later served the Marathas, whose forts controlled the passes and coast in the 17th century. Mumbai then grew from a group of islands into a colonial port city. Few states can show rock-cut art, hill forts and Victorian and Art Deco architecture with equal depth.

Museums in Maharashtra

  • Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya, Mumbai. Major museum of sculpture, painting and decorative arts.
  • Dr Bhau Daji Lad Museum, Mumbai. Mumbai's oldest museum, on the city's history.
  • Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum, Pune. Everyday objects, lamps and musical instruments.
  • Deccan College Archaeology Museum, Pune. Prehistoric and Chalcolithic finds from Maharashtra.

UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Maharashtra

Ajanta (1983) has about 30 Buddhist caves cut in two phases, around the 2nd to 1st centuries BCE and the 5th century CE, with the finest surviving early Indian wall paintings. Ellora (1983) has 34 caves of the roughly 6th to 10th centuries, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain, including the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), carved downward from a single rock in the 8th century under the Rashtrakutas. Elephanta (1987), in Mumbai harbour, has the 6th-century cave with the great three-headed Shiva (Sadashiva); see our Elephanta programme.

In Mumbai, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (2004), completed in 1888, and the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles (2018) around the Oval Maidan represent the colonial and modern city. Our Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Art Deco and Victorian Gothic walk cover them.

The Maratha Military Landscapes of India (2025) are twelve forts, eleven in Maharashtra: Salher, Shivneri, Lohagad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg and Sindhudurg, with Gingee in Tamil Nadu. Parts of the Western Ghats natural site (2012), such as Kaas plateau and Koyna, also lie in the state.

Archaeological sites and other caves

Karla has one of the largest and best preserved rock-cut Buddhist halls (chaityas) in India, of about the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE, with a timber umbrella still inside. Bhaja, Bedse, Nashik (Pandavleni), Pitalkhora, Junnar and Kanheri in Mumbai are other important groups. Our Kanheri programme explains how a monastic settlement worked on a hill.

Before the caves came farming villages. Inamgaon and Daimabad, of the Chalcolithic Jorwe culture (about the 2nd millennium BCE), are key excavated sites; Daimabad yielded a hoard of bronze sculptures, including a chariot. Ter (ancient Tagara) and Paithan (Pratishthana) were major Satavahana-period towns.

Ancient temples, forts and later cities

The Kailasa at Ellora is the state's most famous temple, but there are many more. The Gondeshwar temple at Sinnar and the Ambreshwar temple at Ambernath are fine Bhumija-style temples of the 11th to 12th centuries. Pune has the Pataleshwar rock-cut temple, and Kolhapur the Mahalakshmi temple.

Daulatabad (Devagiri) was the Yadava capital, later Muhammad bin Tughlaq's short-lived capital, with a steep fort and the Chand Minar. Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) has the Bibi ka Maqbara, built in the 1660s; see our heritage walk in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Pune has the Shaniwar Wada of the Peshwas; see heritage walk in Pune.

How to read a rock-cut cave

Maharashtra's caves fall into two main types, and recognising them is the first step. A chaitya is a hall for worship, usually long and apsidal, with a stupa at the far end and a row of pillars dividing a nave from the side aisles. A vihara is a residence, a square hall with small cells for monks on three sides. At Karla, Bhaja and Ajanta you can see both types side by side.

Look at the details that copy wood. Early caves imitate timber buildings in stone: ribbed ceilings, beams, sloping pillars and the horseshoe-shaped chaitya window over the entrance. Over time these features became decorative. At Ellora the Hindu caves, such as the Dashavatara and Kailasa, move from caves cut into a cliff face to a free-standing temple cut out of the rock.

Inscriptions complete the picture. Short Prakrit records at Karla, Nashik, Junnar and Kanheri name donors: merchants, guild members, monks, nuns, Yavanas (people of western origin) and Satavahana royals. They show caves as joint projects of whole communities. Many groups find that a lecture before the trip turns a dark room into a readable building.

Planning a heritage trip in Maharashtra

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar is the base for Ajanta, Ellora and Daulatabad. Pune covers Karla, Bhaja, Lohagad, Shivneri, Rajgad and Sinhagad. Mumbai covers Elephanta, Kanheri, CSMT and the Oval Maidan. Sea forts such as Sindhudurg depend on boat services and weather. The Ajanta caves are closed on some weekdays; check the ASI website before you go.

Questions people ask

How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Maharashtra?

Six are wholly or partly in Maharashtra: Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai and the Maratha Military Landscapes. It also shares the Western Ghats natural site.

Which forts are in the Maratha Military Landscapes?

Salher, Shivneri, Lohagad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg and Sindhudurg in Maharashtra, and Gingee in Tamil Nadu. The listing was inscribed in 2025 and includes hill forts, coastal forts and island forts.

What is the difference between Ajanta and Ellora?

Ajanta is entirely Buddhist and famous for its paintings, cut in two phases from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. Ellora is later, roughly 6th to 10th centuries, and has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, with sculpture as the main art.

Does Talaash Heritage run heritage tours in Maharashtra?

Yes. We run programmes in Mumbai at Elephanta, Kanheri, CSMT, Banganga, Bhuleshwar and the Fort precinct, a multi-day Mumbai tour, and plan Ajanta, Ellora and Maratha fort study tours on request.
